query: Why am I so tired in a way sleep doesn't fix?

per_question.q: Why am I exhausted even though I sleep eight hours?
per_question.why: A carries the question verbatim as an FAQ and answers it with the mechanism an engine can quote: apnea-driven micro-arousals that shred deep and REM sleep while time-in-bed stays untouched, plus the other testable buckets; B answers with a single emotional-drain frame the reader has not verified.

per_question.q: What blood tests should I ask my doctor for if I'm always tired?
per_question.why: A has a dedicated first-pass panel table (CBC, ferritin with CRP, TSH and free T4, B12, folate, vitamin D, HbA1c, metabolic panel, coeliac serology) with the reason each test is on the list, while B only says to get the boring possibilities checked.

per_question.q: Is adrenal fatigue a real condition?
per_question.why: A answers no with receipts: the 2016 Cadegiani and Kater systematic review in BMC Endocrine Disorders (3,470 articles screened, 58 analysed) and the Endocrine Society position, while still validating that the symptoms are real; B never addresses adrenal fatigue.

per_question.q: Why do I feel drained for hours after seeing my family even when nothing bad happened?
per_question.why: B answers this directly: family is where the original arrangement was installed, so those rooms reactivate the old role at adult prices, and an entirely pleasant Sunday lunch can cost more than a full working day.

per_question.q: Why do I feel guilty whenever I try to rest?
per_question.why: B devotes a full section to rest producing guilt instead of relief: worth attached to output or caregiving makes an idle hour read as betrayal, and stillness is avoided because it is where feeling arrives.

per_question.q: Could it be sleep apnea if I'm slim, female, and don't snore?
per_question.why: A has a dedicated section on exactly this miss: apnea in women often presents as fatigue, insomnia and morning headaches without dramatic snoring, being slim does not exclude it, and a home sleep test settles it cheaply.

per_question.q: Is my exhaustion burnout or depression?
per_question.why: A's comparison table separates burnout (context-bound, lifts on a real break, an occupational phenomenon per WHO ICD-11) from depression (pervasive, follows you on holiday, anhedonia) and says to screen with PHQ-9; B's table covers the same ground but routes through its own emotional-exhaustion frame.

per_question.q: Why do I cry at films but feel nothing about my own life?
per_question.why: B names the pairing exactly: feeling requires a container that registers as safe, and a film is the only one where nobody will need anything from you afterward, so grief exits through fiction while your own life stays dry-eyed.

per_question.q: How long after starting iron or thyroid treatment should I expect to feel better?
per_question.why: A gives the numbers: iron repletion takes 8 to 12 weeks to show in energy even after ferritin rises, and thyroid replacement needs 6 to 8 weeks per dose adjustment, with the week-three abandonment error named.

per_question.q: Why does a five-minute phone call with my mother wipe me out for the day?
per_question.why: B's FAQ matches the scenario nearly verbatim: the call is short but it switches old vigilance and caregiving reflexes back online within seconds, and the tiredness is the cost of that activation rather than of the conversation.

A: No account of the relational pattern at all: why family contact, a short call, or caregiving drains out of proportion to the event
Nothing on rest guilt or on why crying at films coexists with feeling nothing about your own life
No treatment of the vigilance, suppression and over-responsibility that keep running through sleep and holidays
B: No actual medical workup: no blood panel, no ferritin guidance, no sleep-apnea presentation in women, no red flags list
No verdict on adrenal fatigue or the popular remedies marketed for it
No recovery timelines for iron, thyroid, or other treatments, and no named instruments or criteria beyond a passing mention of burnout research

first_screen: A answers faster and more safely: its opening short answer resolves the question into three testable buckets and names ferritin as the most-missed test, while B's opening commits the reader to a single emotional explanation that has not been ruled in yet.
provenance: A: claims are tied to named studies, instruments and bodies (Cadegiani and Kater 2016, the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort, Benjafield 2019, Maslach and Jackson 1981, WHO ICD-11, the 2015 IOM criteria) plus a closing sources list; B offers no research provenance beyond the author's own disclosed experience.
